title_english: Super Mario Bros. Ground Theme (Ground BGM)
research_notes: Officially 'Ground Theme' or 'Ground BGM'; first heard in World 1-1 of Super Mario Bros., released 13 September 1985. One of six themes Kondo wrote for the game. Added to the US National Recording Registry in 2023 (Library of Congress essay by David Gibson). Year 1985 is the game release year.

composer: Hirokazu Tanaka (arrangement); traditional Russian melody Korobeiniki
secondary_associations: Tetris (Nintendo Game Boy) | Russian folk song Korobeiniki
research_notes: 1989 Game Boy Tetris 'Type A' accompaniment arranged by Hirokazu Tanaka from the 19th-century Russian folk song Korobeiniki. Earlier Korobeiniki arrangements appeared in Spectrum HoloByte Apple IIGS and Mac Tetris versions. The Tetris Company has required the tune in every version since 2002 and holds a sound trademark on this variation. The original folk song is a separate europe.csv record. Year 1989 is the Game Boy release/arrangement year. Country is Japan (the game arrangement), not Russia.

VGMdb-style preservation wiki lists Overworld BGM by Koji Kondo, released 21 February 1986, and says the title comes from the Famicom 20th Anniversary soundtrack. The game article says Kondo composed the music and that the game was released in Japan on 21 February 1986. The Nintendo interview confirms Kondo wrote the opening from the overworld music after Boléro could not be used. The Ground Theme from Super Mario Bros. was already in this file under another title, so it was not repeated. Second Kondo association is this Zelda theme only.

The Wikipedia music article lists プレリュード (Prelude) as a Nobuo Uematsu track from Final Fantasy and cites a reference line 'Game: Final Fantasy (1987, Square, NES)'. VGMPF dates the Prelude release 18 December 1987 and says it was first released in Japan under that katakana title. MusicBrainz names Uematsu as composer. Uematsu was working in Tokyo for Square when he wrote the early Final Fantasy music, which is the country basis.

title_original: オープニング・テーマ
research_notes: The music article's track list gives オープニング・テーマ as Opening Theme from Final Fantasy I, composed by Nobuo Uematsu. The same article's references identify Final Fantasy as a 1987 Square NES game. Second Uematsu title. The 1989 album All Sounds of Final Fantasy I•II is a later release of this cue.

The music article lists メイン・テーマ (Main Theme) among the Final Fantasy I cues by Nobuo Uematsu and says the Main Theme from Final Fantasy I was later performed at the 2006 Press Start concert in Tokyo. Third Uematsu title. Year 1987 follows the article's reference to the 1987 game rather than the 1989 album.

title_original: Shadow of the Colossus: Roar of the Earth
title_english: ワンダと巨像 大地の咆哮
research_notes: The game article's music section says Kow Otani composed the soundtrack and that the album Shadow of the Colossus: Roar of the Earth was released 7 December 2005, recorded at Victor Studio. The Japanese game date on that page is 27 October 2005. Otani's article says he scored the game in 2005. The PlayStation Blog interview confirms he composed the score. This record is the score as released, not one cue. Piano is named on the soundtrack-credit page returned with the search (bestofvgm), which also lists orchestra and chorus; that credit page is used only for instrumentation and is not the source_url.

The soundtrack track list gives the Japanese title 時の回廊 and the English title Corridors of Time. The Music column is blank. The same article says the majority of the tracks were composed by Yasunori Mitsuda and that Nobuo Uematsu's ten tracks are the ones marked Uematsu. Album release date on that page is 25 March 1995. The game article says Chrono Trigger was developed and published by Square in 1995 and was the second best-selling game of 1995 in Japan. Country is taken from that Japan sales sentence and from Square as the Japanese developer named on the game page.

Track list title サラのテーマ / Schala's Theme, Music column blank. The article attributes unmarked tracks to Yasunori Mitsuda and marks Nobuo Uematsu's contributions in the Music column. Soundtrack released 25 March 1995. Japan is stated on the game article as the 1995 sales market.

The article names 遥かなる時の彼方へ / To Far Away Times as a track Mitsuda attributed to a dream, and the original soundtrack track list includes it with a blank Music column. Album released 25 March 1995 by NTT Publishing. The game article places the 1995 release in the Japanese sales chart. Third Mitsuda title; Uematsu tracks on the same album were not added because three Uematsu titles were already in the file.
